title_en: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease: The NOPARK Randomized Clinical Trial.
title_zh: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease: The NOPARK Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Nicotinamide riboside, a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide precursor, has been proposed as a potential disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson disease based on preclinical and early studies. Whether prolonged oral nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease is unknown. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease compared with placebo. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial conducted at 11 centers in Norway. Eligible participants were patients aged 35 years or older with Parkinson disease diagnosed within 2 years before enrollment, Hoehn and Yahr disease stage less than 3, abnormal dopamine transporter scintigraphy findings confirming dopaminergic nigrostriatal denervation, and stable dopaminergic treatment before enrollment. Of 537 screened individuals, 410 were randomized from May 6, 2020, to June 20, 2024, and 393 were included in the primary analysis. Final follow-up was completed on June 19, 2025. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to receive oral nicotinamide riboside, 500 mg twice daily (n = 206), or matching placebo (n = 204) for 52 weeks. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was change from baseline to week 52 in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale total score (MDS-UPDRS parts I-III; range, 0-236, with higher scores indicating more severe disease; clinically important differences for improvement and worsening, 6.7 and 5.2 points, respectively), analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures. The 5 key secondary outcomes were the individual parts I, II, and III of the MDS-UPDRS; dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography brain imaging findings; and the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale score (NMSS; range, 0-360, with higher scores indicating greater nonmotor symptom burden). RESULTS: Among the 393 participants in the primary analysis, the mean age was 65.6 (SD, 9.4) years and 133 (34%) were female. At week 52, the total MDS-UPDRS score increased by 2.45 (95% CI, 0.80-4.10) points with nicotinamide riboside and decreased by 0.27 (95% CI, -1.95 to 1.40) points with placebo, yielding an adjusted mean difference of 2.72 points (95% CI, 0.47-4.98 points; P = .02), favoring placebo. Of the 5 prespecified key secondary outcomes, 4 showed no significant difference, but nonmotor symptom burden worsened more with nicotinamide riboside (NMSS score adjusted mean difference, 4.22 [95% CI, 1.07-7.37] points; P = .009). Serious adverse events occurred in 17 (8.3%) of 205 participants receiving nicotinamide riboside and 29 (14.1%) of 205 receiving placebo in the safety population. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among patients with early Parkinson disease, nicotinamide riboside treatment for 52 weeks did not improve clinical outcomes and was associated with worse clinical outcomes than placebo. These findings do not support nicotinamide riboside as a disease-modifying treatment for Parkinson disease. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03568968.

title_en: The glymphatic-lymphatic axis: known pathways, open questions, and emerging roles in neurodegeneration.
title_zh: The glymphatic-lymphatic axis: known pathways, open questions, and emerging roles in neurodegeneration.
abstract: The discovery of the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels has transformed our understanding of brain fluid homeostasis and central-peripheral communication, highlighting the critical role of cerebrospinal fluid in brain clearance. While substantial progress has been made in defining the structural components and physiological regulators of brain clearance, major uncertainties remain regarding (1) how these systems interact as an integrated physiological network, (2) how they fail in disease, and (3) whether they can be therapeutically manipulated. In this review, we first summarize the anatomical and physiological organization of the glymphatic-lymphatic axis, with particular emphasis on its regulatory mechanisms in light of rapid advances in this field. We then discuss how the glymphatic-lymphatic axis functionally integrates with peripheral immune and metabolic systems and describe how impairment of these clearance pathways is associated with the accumulation of pathological proteins, neuroinflammation, and vascular dysfunction and may contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and biomarkers targeting the glymphatic-lymphatic axis. By redefining the central-peripheral crosstalk, the glymphatic-lymphatic axis provides a unifying framework for understanding brain clearance, neurodegeneration, and future therapeutic interventions.

title_en: Bacteria-Derived 1-Allylpiperazine Alleviates Symptoms of Parkinson's Disease Model by Promoting Autophagy.
title_zh: Bacteria-Derived 1-Allylpiperazine Alleviates Symptoms of Parkinson's Disease Model by Promoting Autophagy.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no available disease-modifying therapies. Given their diverse health-promoting properties, probiotics have emerged as a potential neuroprotective strategy. Through screening in transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) models of alpha-synuclein (alpha-syn)-induced PD, we identified the Escherichia coli (E. coli) strain E8 as a candidate that effectively suppressed dendritic degeneration and motor deficits. These neuroprotective improvements were attributed to the reduction of alpha-syn aggregation, which was mechanistically associated with E8's ability to promote autophagy. Metabolomic profiling further pinpointed 1-allylpiperazine (1-ALPP) as a bioactive metabolite responsible for rescuing PD-related impairments, which was sufficient to recapitulate the autophagy activation induced by E8. Subsequent mechanistic studies revealed that 1-ALPP activated autophagy through the AMPK/mTOR/HLH-30 pathway. Notably, 1-ALPP effectively inhibited alpha-syn fibrillogenesis and cytotoxicity in a dose-dependent manner, potentially via the inhibition of alpha-syn liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Molecular simulations demonstrated that 1-ALPP binds to alpha-syn, thereby preventing the critical conformational changes required for fibril formation. Strikingly, the protective effects of E8 against PD phenotypes were intergenerationally inherited, persisting for two generations in an hpl-2-dependent manner.

title_en: H4K12 Lactylation Impairs Dopaminergic Neuron Energy Metabolism via the HIF-1alpha/NDUFS1 Pathway in Parkinson's Disease.
title_zh: H4K12 Lactylation Impairs Dopaminergic Neuron Energy Metabolism via the HIF-1alpha/NDUFS1 Pathway in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra, with mitochondrial dysfunction central to its pathology. Recent studies have linked lactate-accumulating in PD due to mitochondrial dysfunction-to disease mechanisms through lactylation, a novel post-translational modification. However, the specific pathogenic role of lactylation in PD remains unclear. Here, H4K12 was identified as a key histone lactylation site and its role in PD pathogenesis was investigated. Plasma lactate and global histone lactylation were elevated in 83 PD patients compared with 83 Health controls. Consistently, lactate and H4K12la were upregulated in both PD mouse and cell models. Genome-wide CUT&Tag and RNA sequencing revealed that H4K12la enrichment at the HIF-1alpha promoter upregulates HIF-1alpha, which in turn represses NDUFS1 via direct promoter binding, impairing mitochondrial respiration and disrupted cellular energy supply. Upstream, P300 was identified as a critical catalyst of H4K12la; P300 directly bound to and sustained H4K12la levels. Collectively, these findings delineate a pathogenic signaling axis-the P300/H4K12la/HIF-1alpha/NDUFS1 axis-that disrupts energy homeostasis in DA neurons. Importantly, the pharmacological inhibition of this axis with 2-deoxy-D-glucose or PX-478 rescued motor deficits in PD model mice, thereby highlighting its therapeutic potential for PD.

title_en: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders.
title_zh: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders.
abstract: Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson's disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound's mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

title_en: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson's disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice.
title_zh: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson's disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a systemic disorder linked to gut dysbiosis, yet key microbiota-regulated metabolites remain unclear. Here, we observe elevated taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) in patients with PD that correlates with disease severity. Reduced bile salt hydrolase (BSH) gene abundance correlates inversely with circulating TCDCA, consistent with altered bile acid deconjugation. Exogenous TCDCA correlates with aggravated motor and gastrointestinal deficits, impaired blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and accelerated dopaminergic neurodegeneration in a PD mouse model. Mechanistically, TCDCA links to TGR5 signaling activation in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), alongside PKCalpha-dependent mitochondrial apoptosis and BBB disruption. VSMC-specific Tgr5 deletion coincides with neurovascular protection. Supplementation with a BSH-high Lactobacillus reuteri strain reduces TCDCA concentrations, improves gut and BBB integrity, mitigates inflammation, and alleviates PD-like phenotypes in a BSH-dependent manner. These data support a gut-BBB-brain axis linked to PD, identifying TCDCA as a candidate pathological marker.

title_en: Renal stress-associated extracellular vesicle signaling linked to lysosomal cathepsin D and NEK7-NLRP3 neuroinflammation.
title_zh: Renal stress-associated extracellular vesicle signaling linked to lysosomal cathepsin D and NEK7-NLRP3 neuroinflammation.
abstract: Systemic exposure to neurotoxins such as 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) affects both the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral organs; however, the contribution of peripheral organ stress to neuroinflammation remains incompletely understood. Here, we propose a peripheral-to-central signaling mechanism in which renal stress-associated extracellular vesicles (EVs) are linked to microglial inflammasome activation. Using computational and biochemical approaches, cathepsin D (CTSD) was identified as a molecular target of the MPTP metabolite 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP +). MPP + accumulated in renal tissue and was associated with lysosomal stress and tubular injury, accompanied by increased release of circulating EVs enriched with renal injury markers. Pharmacological inhibition of pepstatin A-sensitive lysosomal protease activity attenuated renal injury and EV release. MPTP exposure was also associated with blood-brain barrier disruption, potentially permitting circulating EV-associated signaling to influence the CNS. Plasma-derived EVs isolated under MPTP-treated conditions were associated with increased microglial activation, whereas pharmacological inhibition of EV biogenesis attenuated this response. Mechanistically, EV exposure was associated with inflammatory responses involving NIMA-related kinase 7 (NEK7)-NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3-associated inflammatory signaling and IL-1beta maturation. Consistent with these findings, NEK7 deficiency attenuated microglial activation and dopaminergic neuron loss in vivo. Together, these findings suggest that renal stress-associated EVs may be involved in linking peripheral stress to central neuroinflammatory responses. This study provides a tentative but verifiable framework for renal stress-EV-inflammasome communication in toxin-induced neuroinflammation.

title_en: A second-generation "hypoxia in a pill" rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes across distinct mouse models.
title_zh: A second-generation "hypoxia in a pill" rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes across distinct mouse models.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: A growing body of preclinical research is demonstrating the therapeutic potential of chronic, continuous hypoxia (11% FIO(2)) for rare and common diseases. However, the chronic delivery of hypoxic gas poses both practical challenges and long-term safety concerns. We previously introduced a small-molecule, "hypoxia-in-a-pill" combining a hemoglobin affinity enhancer (GBT440) to limit oxygen delivery with a HIF-2alpha inhibitor (PT2399) to prevent detrimental compensatory erythropoiesis. Although this small-molecule regimen extended the lifespan of the Ndufs4 knockout (KO) mouse model of mitochondrial complex I deficiency and Leigh syndrome, its efficacy did not match chronic 11% FIO(2). Here we optimize this regimen using GBT601, a second-generation hemoglobin affinity enhancer with longer half-life and greater hemoglobin occupancy, and show it rescues key neurodegenerative phenotypes in multiple models. When we initiate therapy in 50 d old Ndufs4 KO mice with advanced disease, GBT601 monotherapy alleviated neurological disease phenotypes and extended median lifespan from 62 to 105 d, while dual therapy with the GBT601/PT2399 combination extended median lifespan to 158 d. When initiated after onset of advanced disease in a mouse model of Friedreich's ataxia, the combination halted further progression of motor phenotypes. In a mouse model of Parkinson's disease due to alpha-synuclein toxicity, initiating the GBT601/PT2399 combination after onset of motor dysfunction attenuates brain hyperoxia and lipid peroxidation and reverses motor phenotypes. Importantly, the combination maintained body weight without inducing any signs of pulmonary hypertension. Our findings motivate further preclinical and clinical evaluation of our "hypoxia in a pill" approach for diseases with high unmet need.

title_en: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
title_zh: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

title_en: Relationship Between Braak and Clinical Stage in Autopsy-Confirmed Parkinson Disease: A UK Brain Bank Study.
title_zh: Relationship Between Braak and Clinical Stage in Autopsy-Confirmed Parkinson Disease: A UK Brain Bank Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The gold standard for Parkinson disease (PD) diagnosis is postmortem examination, based on the presence and distribution of pathologic alpha-synuclein (Lewy pathology) across brain regions. Whether pathologic alpha-synuclein Braak staging reflects clinical disease progression remains uncertain. We examined the relationship between Braak stage with clinical indices of PD progression in an autopsy-proven cohort. METHODS: We performed a retrospective clinicopathologic analysis of autopsy-confirmed PD cases from the Parkinson's UK Brain Bank (Imperial College London). Clinical records were systematically reviewed to extract age at symptom onset, disease duration, brain weight, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage at death, and key clinical features. Normality was assessed using Shapiro-Wilk tests; comparisons across Braak stages used Kruskal-Wallis tests. Correlations with Braak stage were examined using Spearman correlation with 95% CIs. Prevalence of major copathologies was summarized descriptively. RESULTS: Of 119 clinically diagnosed PD cases, we included all 61 with autopsy confirmation and available Braak staging. Mean +/- SD age at death was 79.1 +/- 7.4 years, disease duration was 13.5 +/- 5.8 years, H&Y stage at death was 4.0 +/- 0.8, and brain weight was 1,234.2 +/- 108 g. Braak stage was not correlated with H&Y at death (rho = 0.146, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.39, p = 0.262), age at death (rho = -0.210, 95% CI -0.47 to 0.07, p = 0.104), disease duration (rho = 0.035, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.29, p = 0.787), or brain weight (rho = 0.2, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.42, p = 0.139). There were no differences across Braak stages in disease duration (p = 0.925), age at death (p = 0.356), brain weight (p = 0.279), or H&Y stage (p = 0.603). By contrast, brain weight correlated negatively with age at death (rho = -0.352, 95% CI -0.57 to -0.09, p = 0.005). Copathologies were common, including entorhinal/allocortical tau (B1-B2) in 82%, small vessel disease in 60%, beta-amyloid (Thal >/=1) in 58%, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy in 25%. The prevalence of copathologies did not differ across Braak stages. DISCUSSION: Braak stage was not associated with H&Y at death, disease duration, age at death, or brain weight in autopsy-proven PD patients. These findings provide evidence that pathologic alpha-synuclein-based staging does not represent a model of clinical progression in PD. The quantification of both monomeric and pathologic alpha-synuclein may be needed to overcome the clinical limitations of pathology-based staging.

title_en: Plasma Lipid Remodeling across Preclinical Burden, Disease Onset, and Early Motor Severity in Huntington's Disease.
title_zh: Plasma Lipid Remodeling across Preclinical Burden, Disease Onset, and Early Motor Severity in Huntington's Disease.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Huntington's disease (HD) evolves silently for years before motor onset, yet the systemic metabolic alterations accompanying cumulative exposure to mutant huntingtin and disease progression remain poorly understood. We aimed to identify plasma metabolic signatures associated with disease burden, disease onset and motor severity in HD. METHODS: Mutation carriers with 36 or more cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) repeats in the HTT gene were prospectively recruited and classified as premanifest or early manifest. Fasting plasma samples were analyzed using targeted metabolomics and lipidomics. Linear models adjusted for covariates were used to investigate associations with CAG-Age Product (CAP) score, disease stage, and motor severity (Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale total motor score). Lipid-class enrichment, acyl-chain enrichment and composite lipid score analyses were performed to characterize coordinated metabolic remodeling. RESULTS: Ninety-three mutation carriers (54 premanifest and 39 early manifest individuals) were included. Increasing CAP scores were associated with coordinated enrichment of eicosapentaenoic (20:5) and docosahexaenoic (22:6) acid-containing phospholipids together with depletion of triglycerides. In contrast, disease onset was characterized by enrichment of triglycerides and of lipids containing palmitate, palmitoleate, and arachidonate, accompanied by an increased palmitoleate-to-palmitate ratio of cholesteryl esters. In early manifest individuals, increasing motor severity was associated with depletion of docosahexaenoic acid-containing phospholipids, an increased phosphatidylserine-to-phosphatidylcholine ratio and reduced circulating acylcarnitines. These findings were supported by composite lipid scores and leave-one-subject-out sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSIONS: HD is associated with coordinated plasma lipid remodeling across disease stages. Distinct lipid signatures characterize cumulative mutant huntingtin exposure, disease onset and motor progression, providing insights into the metabolic consequences of HD. (c) 2026 The Author(s). title_en: Cerebellar Network Organization in Parkinson's Disease: Functional Connectivity across Motor and Cognitive Circuits.
title_zh: Cerebellar Network Organization in Parkinson's Disease: Functional Connectivity across Motor and Cognitive Circuits.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: BACKGROUND: The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to cognitive reserve and network organization in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, the relationship of cerebello-cortical and cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity with cognitive status and nigrostriatal integrity remains incompletely understood. METHODS: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 172 participants with PD in the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative were analyzed. Cerebello-basal ganglia and cerebello-cortical connectivity were investigated using region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel approaches. Cerebellar connectivity was examined in relation to cognitive status, age, disease duration, motor severity, dopaminergic medication exposure, and contralateral putaminal striatal binding ratio (SBR). RESULTS: PD participants demonstrated robust positive cerebello-basal ganglia connectivity, particularly between lobule VI/vermis VI and the pallidum. Greater age was associated with widespread reductions in cerebello-basal ganglia coupling. Longer disease duration was associated with stronger connectivity within cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits, and among cognitively unimpaired participants, stronger lobule V connectivity with temporal regions. After adjustment for contralateral putaminal SBR, cognitively unimpaired participants generally demonstrated greater connectivity between left cerebellar regions and frontal networks, whereas cognitively impaired participants showed greater connectivity from posterior cerebellar and vermal regions, including regions implicated in cognitive processing, to temporal, parahippocampal, occipital, parietal, and somatosensory regions. CONCLUSIONS: Cerebellar functional connectivity in PD shows region-specific differences across cognitive status rather than uniform network loss with cognitive impairment. These findings support further investigation of cerebellar functional connectivity as a candidate biomarker of cognitive resilience and network adaptation in PD. (c) 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title_en: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
title_zh: A GLP-1/apelin dual receptor agonist shows neuroprotective effects in the MPTP mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) class of drugs is on the market to treat diabetes and obesity. GLP-1 drugs have also shown neuroprotective effects in animal models and clinical trials in PD patients. Apelin (APJ) is an adipokine peptide hormone with neuroprotective actions in preclinical studies. Here, we test the effects of a rationally designed bifunctional peptide, namely ELA (exendin-4-linker-apelin), in the MPTP mouse model of PD. The single GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide was used as a comparator. Motor activity was improved by both drugs (open field, pole test, Rotarod), and the inflammation response was reduced (activation of microglia and astrocytes, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels). In addition, synapse numbers were improved in the striatum (Golgi strain, TEM), expression of synapse-associated proteins was enhanced, alongside reduced expression of genes that increase mitochondrial fission. Mitochondrial fusion gene expressions (Opa1, Mfn2, Drp1) and mitochondrial morphology were also normalized (TEM). ELA was superior to liraglutide in some, but not all, parameters measured. The results suggest that the rational design of bifunctional peptides targeting both GLP-1 and APJ pathways-with optimized pharmacokinetics and enhanced blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability-merits further investigation as a strategy for developing more effective treatments for PD.

title_en: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.
title_zh: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.
journal: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. PURPOSE: CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity. METHODS: Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. RESULTS: The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy. CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

title_en: FA-MFMR: a multivariable functional Mendelian randomization method that accounts for correlated longitudinal exposures via factor augmentation.
title_zh: FA-MFMR: a multivariable functional Mendelian randomization method that accounts for correlated longitudinal exposures via factor augmentation.
abstract: MOTIVATION: Mendelian randomization (MR) is widely used for causal inference using genetic data, yet most existing MR methods treat exposures as static and have limited capacity to analyze longitudinal measurements. In many biomedical studies, multiple exposures evolve over time, are strongly correlated, and share unobserved temporal structure. Ignoring these features can lead to unstable estimation and reduced power. RESULTS: We propose factor-augmented multivariable functional Mendelian randomization (FA-MFMR) for estimating time-varying causal effects of multiple longitudinal exposures. FA-MFMR integrates genetic instruments with functional representations of exposure trajectories and a low-dimensional factor structure to capture shared temporal patterns. By separating common temporal variation from exposure-specific components, it mitigates multicollinearity, improves estimation stability, and accommodates sparse causal structures in which some exposures have no effect throughout the observation period. Simulations demonstrate lower estimation error and more efficient uncertainty quantification than competing approaches, particularly for highly correlated and sparsely observed longitudinal exposures. Applied to longitudinal biomarkers in a Parkinson's disease cohort, FA-MFMR characterizes age-dependent patterns in the estimated trajectory-level coefficient functions while highlighting uncertainty in localized effects. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The developed R package and code to reproduce all the results are available at https://github.com/YQHuFD/FA-MFMR. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available online.

title_en: Lactoferrin-modified MSC-derived extracellular vesicles facilitate BBB penetration and enhance gastrodin-induced neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease: involvement of mitophagy.
title_zh: Lactoferrin-modified MSC-derived extracellular vesicles facilitate BBB penetration and enhance gastrodin-induced neuroprotection in Parkinson's disease: involvement of mitophagy.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely impedes neuroprotective agent delivery to the brain in Parkinson's disease (PD). Although gastrodin (Gas) possesses neuroprotective properties, its efficacy is limited by poor BBB permeability. This study aimed to develop a brain-targeted extracellular vesicle (EV) delivery system for Gas and elucidate its neuroprotective mechanisms. METHODS: A brain-targeted EV delivery system was developed using mesenchymal stem cell-derived EVs modified with lactoferrin (Lf). Gas was loaded into Lf-EVs via sonication to construct Lf-EVs-Gas nanocomplexes. The nanocomplexes were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, western blotting, and nano-flow cytometry. Trans-Barrier transport was evaluated using an in vitro Transwell BBB model (hCMEC/D3 cells), while therapeutic efficacy and biodistribution were assessed in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. RESULTS: Lf-EVs-Gas exhibited a typical cup-shaped morphology, with a mean size of 79.08 nm and a drug loading efficiency of 47.08 +/- 4.63%. Lf functionalization significantly enhanced BBB transport, achieving a brain Gas concentration of 10.34 +/- 2.7 ng/g in PD mice versus undetectable levels for free Gas. The targeted system demonstrated superior brain accumulation versus non-targeted vesicles. In 6-OHDA-treated SH-SY5Y cells and MPTP-induced PD mice, the system upregulated tyrosine hydroxylase, reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation, inhibited neuronal apoptosis, and improved motor function. Mechanistically, these protective effects of Lf-EVs-Gas were associated with activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, as evidenced by elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and increased TOMM20/LC3 colocalization. CONCLUSION: Lf-EVs-Gas enhanced the brain delivery of Gas and produced neuroprotective effects in cellular and mouse toxin-based models of PD. These effects were associated with the activation of PINK1-related mitophagy, supporting Lf-modified EVs as a promising brain-targeted delivery platform for Gas. Further studies establishing mechanistic causality, long-term safety, and efficacy in progressive PD models are warranted.

title_en: Dopaminergic state modulates shame and contextual emotional responses in Parkinson's disease.
title_zh: Dopaminergic state modulates shame and contextual emotional responses in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: BackgroundShame is frequent in Parkinson's disease (PD) and negatively affects quality of life, yet its dopaminergic modulation remains unclear.MethodsWe investigated the effect of dopaminergic replacement therapy (DRT) on shame in 41 fluctuating PD patients using an experimental tailored shame induction task. At visit 1, participants were presented with 60 short written scenarios (neutral, non-PD-related shame, PD-related shame). A tailored selection of 12 scenarios (4 per category) was generated in three steps: (1) initial rating of all 60 scenarios on a shame/embarrassment visual analogue scale (VAS); (2) selection of the highest-rated scenarios for shame conditions and lowest-rated scenarios for neutral condition to account for individual emotional relevance; and (3) emotional rating of these scenarios on 10 VAS (fear, sadness, disgust, joy, self- and other-directed anger, shame, embarrassment, guilt, stress) to ensure specificity of shame/embarrassment responses. At visits 2 and 3, patients rated the 12 scenarios once ON- and once OFF-DRT (randomized crossover design) using the same 10 VAS.ResultsIn OFF-DRT state, shame ratings were lower than in ON-DRT for non-PD-related shame scenarios (Zratio = -2.53, p = 0.02), with a similar trend for PD-related shame scenarios (Zratio = -2.02, p = 0.06). Conversely, patients reported higher embarrassment (Zratio = 4.53, p < 0.001), stress (Zratio = 3.49, p < 0.001), and self-directed anger (Zratio = 3.99, p < 0.001) when evaluating scenarios rated as neutral in the ON-DRT state.ConclusionsIn OFF-DRT state, emotional responses showed altered contextual calibration, with reduced shame in shame-eliciting contexts and increased negative emotions in neutral situations. These findings suggest that dopaminergic state may modulate intensity and appraisal processes of emotions.

title_en: Meaningful digital mobility outcomes for people with Parkinson's disease: Insights grounded in diverse lived experience.
title_zh: Meaningful digital mobility outcomes for people with Parkinson's disease: Insights grounded in diverse lived experience.
abstract: BackgroundDigital mobility outcomes (DMOs) have been cited as potential clinical endpoints for trials in Parkinson's disease (PD). Current evidence from the Mobilise-D consortium suggests that selected DMOs are technically valid, with emerging research on their clinical validity. However, regulatory qualification of DMOs requires additional evidence of their meaningfulness to people with PD.ObjectiveTo identify meaningful DMOs by understanding how mobility symptoms impact aspects of health that matter to people with PD.MethodsPurposive sampling recruited a diverse sample of people with PD to participate in semi-structured interviews. Content analysis identified frequent and bothersome mobility symptoms and their impacts on meaningful aspects of health. Twelve experts mapped meaningful symptoms to relevant DMOs through a nominal group consensus.ResultsSeventy-two people with PD participated, inclusive of under-served groups: ethnic minorities (14%) or LGBTQIA + backgrounds (14%), in older age (3%) or with young-onset PD (13%), living rurally (31%) or in a deprived area (19%). Shuffling gait, bradykinesia and balance issues were the most frequent symptoms, and the most bothersome and impactful on meaningful aspects of health (i.e., activities of daily living, life-space mobility, emotional wellbeing) among participants who experienced them. Less frequent, but still highly bothersome and impactful symptoms included freezing of gait, fatigue and weakness. Expert consensus suggested that walking speed, stride length and turn duration were the most relevant DMOs to reflect these meaningful symptoms.ConclusionFindings offer an inclusive, meaningful framework for digital assessment of mobility in PD, grounded in lived experience and consistent with regulatory guidance.

title_en: Technology to remotely capture key elements of swallowing and speech: State of the science in Parkinson's disease.
title_zh: Technology to remotely capture key elements of swallowing and speech: State of the science in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Swallowing and speech impairments are common in Parkinson's disease (PD) and can significantly affect health and quality of life. Traditional methods for assessing and managing these functions rely on in-person visits and large, expensive equipment, which are inaccessible to many patients. Recent advances in health technologies offer opportunities for remote monitoring and assessment, enabling early detection, personalized intervention, and longitudinal tracking of swallowing and speech deficits in PD. This review synthesizes evidence on current and emerging technologies designed to remotely capture key elements of swallowing and speech in patients with PD. We present studies that develop and use wearable uni- and multi-modal sensor-based approaches, biofeedback devices, acoustic analysis through smartphones, and haptic cueing aimed at improving aspects of swallowing and speech. Additionally, we examine the integration of artificial intelligence for automated signal processing and predictive modeling, emphasizing validation studies and clinical feasibility. Challenges related to usability, data quality, adherence, data security, and standardization are discussed alongside opportunities for telehealth-driven care models. By identifying technological innovations and evidence gaps, this review provides a roadmap for future research and clinical implementation of remote swallowing and speech assessment in PD. These advancements have the potential to transform care, reduce healthcare burden, and improve patient outcomes through scalable, non-invasive, and patient-centered solutions for the management of dysphagia and dysarthria in PD.

title_en: Grid to glide: A simple visual cue that alleviates upper-limb freezing.
title_zh: Grid to glide: A simple visual cue that alleviates upper-limb freezing.
abstract: Freezing of the upper limb (FoUL) is a poorly explored manifestation of Parkinson's disease. This report describes a case of a 54-year-old woman with FoUL predominantly affecting handwriting. Writing on grid paper with small squares (0.5 x 0.5 cm) markedly reduced FoUL frequency. A subsequent daily home-based writing and calligraphic training program led to sustained improvements in handwriting legibility, drawing ability, and transfer to writing on blank paper without the grid, without any change in medication. The immediate response to grid paper suggests that simple visual cueing-possibly by promoting block-letter writing and reducing motor planning complexity-could represent a practical strategy for writing-related FoUL, meriting further systematic investigation.

title_en: Measuring what matters: Evaluating quality of life instruments through the eyes of people with Parkinson's disease.
title_zh: Measuring what matters: Evaluating quality of life instruments through the eyes of people with Parkinson's disease.
abstract: BackgroundMany instruments are used to assess quality of life in people living with Parkinson's disease. However, there is limited understanding of what people living with Parkinson's consider relevant and important when measuring quality of life.AimTo explore what people living with Parkinson's consider relevant and important in the assessment of quality of life.MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted with 31 people living with Parkinson's disease. Participants completed eight instruments, which were used to guide discussion and reflection on what helps and what hinders measuring quality of life in a way that is meaningful to them.ResultsParticipants highlighted a number of features they consider important in the assessment of quality of life. These include being able to select from a wide range of response options, addressing the personal, emotional, and practical impacts of issues, using clear, specific language, and including a balance of questions that address both positive and negative aspects of the Parkinson's experience.ConclusionsThere is a need for instruments that reflect the complex and varied ways Parkinson's disease affects individuals. While existing questionnaires incorporate some features that support meaningful assessment, participants also identified features that may hinder the extent to which quality of life is adequately captured and that warrant further refinement. Incorporating feedback from people with lived experience may help inform future evaluation and refinement of quality of life measures in research and care.

title_en: Considerations for therapeutic targets for clinical trials in biomarker-characterized prodromal Parkinson's disease populations.
title_zh: Considerations for therapeutic targets for clinical trials in biomarker-characterized prodromal Parkinson's disease populations.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a growing public health problem and biologically targeted therapeutics (BTTs) that slow disease progression are urgently needed. However, the development of effective BTTs is challenging as PD is a clinically defined syndrome with pathobiological heterogeneity and the pathobiological process begins many years before the onset of clinically detectable motor symptoms. Testing BTTs in a biomarker-defined population at an earlier stage in the disease course, before a clinical PD diagnosis, may be the key to achieving this objective. The recent emergence of biological definitions of neuronal alpha-synuclein disease (NSD) and research frameworks for staging disease represent the first step towards testing BTTs in biomarker-defined prodromal populations. While biomarker-defined populations are essential for implementing precision therapeutic approaches, selecting and prioritizing BTTs for testing in early-stage populations is also critical, and requires consideration of biological relevance, safety, and operational feasibility. Here, in preparation for such studies, we review the landscape of publicly available PD BTTs organized by mechanistic pathways and targets, and summarize scientific, safety, and operational considerations relevant to early-stage, biomarker-defined trials targeting NSD participants prior to PD clinical diagnosis. Recognizing that there are shared biological mechanisms across neurodegenerative disorders, we complement this review of the PD therapeutic target landscape with a review of publicly available Alzheimer's dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis BTTs and provide a comprehensive list of agents for reference.
